1. Introduction¶

Research Question¶

I want to explore data on a wide variety of video games to understand what factors most influence a game's success. The goal of this project is to build a predictive model that performs best when estimating Review Score for new or unseen games. By using information such as platform features (handheld, multiplayer, online support), gameplay length statistics, genre, publisher, and licensing status, we can gain insights into what makes a game highly rated. With our best-performing model, we can also explore the relationships between these variables and identify the key drivers behind a game's critical reception.

Research Motivation¶

Everyone loves playing video games. Whether we’re playing for fun, competing with our friends, or just to relax, we all have some games that we love. This project is interesting because it helps us understand what makes a game good in the eyes of reviewers. If we can predict review scores, game creators might be able to use that to make better games, and players can know which games might be worth checking out. It’s also just interesting to look at real data and find out what makes some games stand out more than others. Video games are prime in todays entertainment, influencing not just how we spend our free time, but also shaping trends in technology. Predicting a game’s potential success can help developers and publishers make informed decisions during production and marketing. For consumers, these insights could guide smarter purchase decisions. By analyzing a wide range of features — from playtime to platform characteristics — and building a predictive model of Review Score, I aim to discover what attributes are most associated with positively reviewed games. This can also benefit game studios aiming to optimize game design or target specific audience expectations.

2. Dataset Discussion¶

Defintions:¶

Features.Max Players: the maximum number of players that can play the game at once

Features.Online?: whether the game supports online gameplay (True/False)

Metadata.Genres: the category or style of the game (e.g., Action, Sports, Strategy)

Metrics.Review Score: average critic review score for the game (out of 100)

Release.Year: the year the game was released

Metrics.Sales: the total number of units the game sold (in millions)

3. Dataset Cleaning¶

Initial Cleaning¶

First, we'd like to drop the Title column from the dataset. While the game title is useful for identification, it doesn't help us when predicting numeric outcomes like review score or modeling gameplay patterns. I also simplified the column names to make them easier to reference in code and to help describe the information each column holds.

Missing Values¶

All of the variable data types in the video games dataset appear to make sense, most columns are either boolean, integers, floats, or strings (object). This means we can work with the dataset without needing to transform incompatible types before analysis. To check for missing data, I checked each column for null values. Almost all columns have complete data except the Publisher column, which contains 264 missing values. These may be games without a listed publisher, and we’ll need to decide whether to fill in these values, drop them, or exclude the column depending on our modeling goals.

Genre Cutoffs¶

Next, it would be reasonable to consider only popular genres in our dataset when building our predictive model. Some genres appear only a handful of times, which may not provide enough data to learn meaningful patterns. Looking at the value counts below, I decided to include only genres that appear at least 50 times in the dataset.

By focusing on these more common genres — such as Action, Sports, Strategy, and RPG combinations — it makes sure that the model will be trained on a solid number of examples, increasing its ability to generalize to new data. Genres with fewer than 50 appearances were excluded from the main analysis or grouped under an "Other" category.

Single Variable Outlier Inspection¶

In [88]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(15, 6))

axes[2].set_title("Average Main + Extras Time")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Looking at each of our explanatory variables, the boxplots suggest that there are some outliers present, especially in numeric features like Sales, Used_Price, and Avg_Main_Extras. To reduce noise in our model, I applied a cutoff to the Avg_Main_Extras column, which contains data about how long it takes to complete the main story plus extras. Any value over 100 hours was considered an outlier and removed from the dataset.

In [89]:
df4 = df3[df3['Avg_Main_Extras'] <= 100]
df3.shape[0] - df4.shape[0]
Out[89]:
6

This means 6 data points were removed due to extreme playtime lengths.

Categorical Variable Inspection¶

In [91]:
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 6))
sns.boxplot(x='Genres', y='Review_Score', data=df4)
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.title("Review Score by Game Genre")
plt.show()

The boxplots reveal that game genres show distinct differences in their review score distributions, with noticeable variation in medians, ranges, and outliers. Sports and Racing titles tend to receive more consistent reviews, while Action-RPG games show greater variability but often score highly. Strategy games, on the other hand, have review scores that are more tightly clustered near the top. These patterns suggest that genre significantly influences review scores and should be considered an important variable in predictive modeling.

4. Preliminary Analysis¶

Variable Transformations¶

I explored several numeric variables — including Sales, Used_Price, and average playtime metrics — to examine their relationship with Review_Score. From the pairplot below, none of the features showed a strong linear correlation with review score. While some mild positive associations appear between longer games and higher scores, the trends are not strong enough to show strong transformations.

In [92]:
numerical_columns = [
    'Sales', 'Used_Price', 'Avg_Main_Story', 'Avg_Main_Extras',
    'Avg_Completionists', 'Review_Score'
]

sns.pairplot(df4[numerical_columns])
plt.show()

The distributions also reveal strong skewness in some features — particularly Sales, which has a long right tail.

nonreg_model = smf.ols('Review_Score ~ Sales + Used_Price + Avg_Main_Story + Avg_Main_Extras + Avg_Completionists', data=df_train_s).fit()
y_test = df_test_s['Review_Score']
y_pred = nonreg_model.predict(df_test_s)
r2_nonreg = r2_score(y_test, y_pred)

6. Best Model Discussion¶

Best Model¶

All three regularized models achieved near-identical R² values, but Ridge Regression was selected due to slightly higher performance (by a minuscule margin).

Best Equation (Ridge)¶

The Ridge model's coefficients reveal that total playtime, handheld status, and genre types like Action or Strategy had the most influence on review score predictions.

Dataset Fit¶

The near-perfect R² indicates that the Ridge model predicts review scores with exceptional accuracy on the test set.

Overfitting¶

Coefficient comparisons between the regularized and non-regularized models were similar, indicating that regularization was not compensating for overfitting—rather, the features already held solid predictive value.

Multicollinearity¶

Correlation analysis showed no explanatory variable pair exceeded the 0.7 threshold, confirming that multicollinearity is not an issue in this model.

Slope Interpretations¶

The most influential variables, based on magnitude of coefficients, were:

Average Playtime

Genre (especially Strategy and Action)

Handheld status

Multiplayer/Online support

Review source/platform

7. Conclusion¶

Relationships Between Variables¶

When examining how different variables relate to a game's review score, I observed several important trends. Genre came up as a particularly influential factor, with distinct median scores and variability across categories—indicating strong differences in how different types of games are received. Additionally, features like game mode, platform, and release year did not exhibit strong linear correlations individually but contributed meaningful variation when combined in a multivariate model. Interaction effects, especially between genre and other variables, suggested trends that couldve needed further exploration, as certain genres may perform differently depending on the context.

Recommendation¶

Based on my analysis, I would recommend using the Ridge regression model, which had the highest test R² value (~0.9981), for predicting review scores. This model provides accurate predictions and is reliable due to its inclusion of multiple explanatory variables and genre dummies. It is particularly well-suited for stakeholders like publishers or developers interested in forecasting review reception based on genre, release year, and gameplay features.

Shortcomings/Caveats¶

Despite the high R² value, there are limitations. For one, several variables did not show strong linear trends in pairwise plots, and I relied heavily on categorical transformations. Also, the high performance may partially reflect overfitting to the available dataset, even though multicollinearity tests showed no major issues. Another limitation is the potential subjectivity in review scores themselves, which can be influenced by factors not captured in this model. Finally, smaller genres or niche game types may not be well represented due to insufficient data.

Future Work¶

To improve the model further, future analysis could include additional features such as marketing budget, user vs. critic score breakdowns, or social media. Exploring non-linear models or other methods could also help catch more interactions within the variable. Finally, expanding the dataset to include more recent games or additional platforms may help ensure the model remains relevant and generalizable.
